utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First of all, a very good morning to everybody before and behind the scenes assisting us in conducting today's status conference. May I ask, please, the representative of the Registrar to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is IT-95-11-A, the Prosecutor versus Milan Martin. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you. May I have the appearances, please. First is the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. It's Michelle Jarvis appearing for the Prosecution, together with Ms. Nicole Lewis and our case manager today, Mr. Sebastiaan van Hooydonk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. On behalf of the Defence team, attorney Predrag Milovancevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask Mr. Martic, himself, can you follow the proceedings in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And at the same time, the question as foreseen in the Rules, do you have any health problems or any complaints on the detention conditions in the UNDU?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not as far as that matter is concerned. All I would like to say -- or actually I would like to say something, with your permission. It will just take a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to say that I'm interested in knowing whether you are going to sincerely review the judgement and our appeal. I'm asking you this question with every right to do so, because the first instance court I can compare only with Dimitrov and the alleged setting fire to the Reichstag earlier on in the last century. Now, the Judges, the Trial Chamber Judges, competed with the Prosecutor to see who the bigger Prosecutor will be. That's the drastic example of it. And if you just delve into the matter, you will see that no matter was taken by the Presiding Judge throughout the year of trial, was positioned and placed to my advantage, not even objectively. All they did was to support the thesis put forward by the Prosecution, and he would be very unhappy if he failed to do that. That's why I consider my trial was a pure inquisition, and you will be able to see that very simply. I was the representative of the nation, of the people, and they had the status of a constitutional people. That people does no longer exist. It's the greatest ethnic cleansing in the 20th century, and nobody was held responsible for that and nobody was held accountable for that, and I don't suppose they will be. I would like to know whether anybody in the United Nations will be held responsible, because we were under UN protection. When I compare our status today and today's status of Kosovo and Metohija, the Albanians, who never were a nation, they were a national minority, they are recognised today, they're being recognised today by various states, and we do not exist. There aren't any more of us. And that's why I'm here. So it wasn't a judgement and sentencing of me, but a judgement of my entire people. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I accept your statement. Of course, you will not expect any answer, but I shall limit myself just to state that, first of all, opposed to the ICJ, International Criminal Jurisdiction, is limited to the question of whether an individual is responsible, and it's not about the state responsibility. So at the end of the day, the question will be for the Appeals Chamber to decide whether or not you yourself, personally, were responsible for those alleged crimes, and in particular you can be assured that in all fairness, the Appeals Chamber will carefully screen the judgement of the Trial Chamber. That's why International Human Rights guarantee a second instance. Before I turn now to the time frame ahead of us in greater detail, I want to move to the motion to order the Prosecution to refile the respondent's brief. First of all, it was filed confidentially. Is there any reason why this was filed confidentially? If not, I would lift the confidentiality. May I hear the Defence on this, having filed this confidentially?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the interpretation I received was the Prosecution brief. I assume you're asking about the Defence brief, our brief. So if you are indeed asking about the Defence brief -- am I right there? Which is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. I referred to the motion filed yesterday. The Prosecutor versus Milan Martic motion to order the Prosecution to refile the respondent's brief. I'm grateful that you alerted us already yesterday so that we discuss it today. And my only question, both in relation to this, as far as the two other documents, I will come back later to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I wasn't clear whether you wanted to hear about our motion or theirs, but there's no reason that it should be confidential, and thank you for asking us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any objections by the Prosecution on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We have no reason to indicate that it should be a closed session matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. And to be abundantly clear, hereby the confidentiality of the motion filed by the Defence of Mr. Martic to order the Prosecution to refile the respondent's brief of 28 February 2008 is lifted. We have the motion before us. You draw, in this motion, your attention to the practice direction on formal requirements for appeals from judgement, and refer in particular to para 5, the last separate paragraph. May I ask the Prosecution in which way they want to respond, if at all, to this?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's convenient, we're prepared to make short oral submissions on the matter today so that you can deal with it immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. If you could start immediately, it would be great.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, in brief, the Prosecution's position is that the motion should be rejected and that the Prosecution's appeal brief should be accepted as having been validly filed. To the extent that the Prosecution should have sought leave to vary the order of its arguments, we apologise to the Chamber for that oversight, and I would seek permission from Your Honour to rectify that by an application here today. Your Honour, the order of the Prosecution's response brief has been guided by the appellant's brief, but we've deviated from it in a couple of respects, and we submit that there are a few reasons why it is appropriate to permit this deviation. First of all, the Prosecution's brief has been ordered in the way it has to promote efficiency, clarity of understanding and coherency in the structure of the break. The alterations were prompted by the fact that we could identify in the appellant's brief a number of overlapping arguments or arguments for which a grouped response was appropriate. We considered that this would be the most efficient way to present our submissions to the Chamber, and in that respect, Your Honour, I would note that using this structure, we were able to come in several thousand words under the word limit. Very briefly, the variations in the order were to begin the brief with a section with summary dismissal arguments which is a cross-cutting theme in our response to the appellant's brief. It was more efficient for us to set out the law and the relevant authorities in one place and to provide illustrations to the Chamber as to the types of arguments throughout the appellant's brief that fall within these categories. Secondly, we've also led our substantive response in the brief with grounds 5 to 8, followed by grounds 1 to 4. And the reason why we've done this, as we've explained in the introduction to our response brief, is that grounds 5 to 8 or our response to those grounds really contains the substantive core of our response to which we then refer to when we reach grounds 1 to 4, so logically, we considered it would aid the Appeal Chamber's comprehension of our response to put the order this way. And thirdly, we have collected together responses to five common or cross-cutting arguments at the beginning of ground 5. Your Honour, the Appeals Chamber has permitted variation in the order of argument from the practice direction where it is to aid the clarity and comprehension of the brief. I would refer Your Honour in that respect to the Krajisnik decision of 31 July, 2007 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down somewhat, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters. To the Oric decision of 3 May 2007, and to a decision of Your Honour Judge Schomburg in this case on the 10th of January, 2008, allowing the appellant to vary his notice of appeal and the order of that to promote greater clarity. Your Honour, for response briefs in particular, notwithstanding the wording of the practice direction, flexibility has been accorded to a responding party to group arguments together in a logical way and to avoid repetition. Your Honour, I would refer you, for example, to response briefs filed in the Brdjanin case, the Kunarac case, the Kvocka case, and the Tuta Stela case where the Prosecution's response briefs provided common arguments or commenced with, as we have in this case, a section dealing with summary dismissal arguments together. In none of these cases was an objection or a complaint raised, notwithstanding the wording of the practice direction. I would also add, Your Honour, that in none of the briefs that I've just mentioned was leave sought to change the order of the argument, but as I've mentioned, to the extent that we should have sought leave for a technical departure from the practice direction, then I would seek to rectify that by making the application now. Your Honour, the second reason why it would be appropriate to dismiss the motion is because notwithstanding the change in the order, we have been at pains to clearly identify throughout our brief which parts of the appellant's brief we are responding to, so that it's easy -- it should be easy for the appellant and the Appeals Chamber to track the correspondence between our arguments and the appellant's arguments, and we've done this through the section headings which refer to the grounds of appeal and also detailed references to paragraph numbers in the appellant's brief. Thirdly, Your Honour, we submit that the appellant has not advanced any compelling reason to justify the Prosecution having to refile the brief. Your Honour, the assertion that it's necessary to consider grounds 1 to 4 prior to grounds 5 to 8, even if this were true, the order of the Prosecution's response brief, of course, does not prevent this. It's up to the Appeals Chamber to determine the most appropriate order for it to consider its judgement, and we've seen in many other cases the Appeals Chamber's judgement following a different order from that set out by the parties in their submission. The other reason advanced by the appellant was that he would be unable to properly order his reply. Your Honour, this hasn't been a problem in other cases, such as Brdjanin and those I've mentioned, where the Prosecution has been permitted to make common or group responses. The Prosecution has no comment on the order in which the appellant structures his reply, provided that he makes it clear which part of the Prosecution's brief he is dealing with. For all those reasons, Your Honour, we submit that the motion filed yesterday should be rejected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I hear the Defence on this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm surprised to hear the position taken by my learned friend, because at the beginning she said that the order was deviated from, the order given with the instructions for practical work, and she would like to have our motion rejected. Now, if the Prosecution has deviated from the order regulated by a certain set of instructions, then they do not have the right to ask that the motion which indicates this deviation be rejected. Secondly, and this is also a very important point, referring to the decision made by Judge Schomburg to allow the appellant to deviate, it does not correspond to this case. The Prosecution made a response to our appeal motion. So these are two qualitatively very different things and cannot be compared. The third point is this: To say that we're dealing with a technical deviation from practice and the order given for practice means to recognise that the instructions have been violated, and then to go on to explain that this was done in order that the Trial Chamber could be able to follow the relationship between the appeal, the Defence, and the Prosecution response, is quite out of order. We really cannot respond to this response on the part of the Prosecution as we would like to do, because with its response, the Prosecution questions the assertions made in our appeals motion, and we have to counteract that challenge and not to present our views about the position principle taken by the Prosecution and how they represent the indictment. So that's the essence of the matter. The Prosecution is challenging our allegations and assertions, whereas it is duty-bound to respect the guidelines and must do so in the order that we did so that in our response, we can present arguments against their motion in our response. So this makes our work much more difficult, and therefore I consider that our motion and the respondent's brief is quite in order and merits being considered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this contribution. Indeed, it's true that this practice direction even reads that the statements and the arguments must be set out -- must be set out and numbered in the same order as the appellant's brief and shall be limited to arguments made in response to the brief. The last part of the sentence does not apply. You refer only to the numbering in the order of the appellant's brief. But in deciding this issue, and as I said, I'm grateful that we received this motion already yesterday. Thus, we were able to look a little bit closer into the documents. We have to ask ourselves: What is the rationale behind this practice direction? This practice direction of 7th March 2002 emanated from the fact that we had numerous response and reply briefs where it was extremely difficult to identify which is in response to what and which is in reply to what, so that it was very difficult to identify what is related to the other document. However, in the case before us, in the Prosecution response brief, and this could, to a certain extent, be read as a request that leave be granted, I draw your attention to para 7 of -- I think this is not confidential, this part, there's nothing confidential in it -- para 7 of the Prosecutor's response brief of 25 February 2008, and there reasons are given why they departed from the order. Normally, I think it would be a matter of courtesy to first ask the Chamber for leave, but under the circumstances you have to take into account the rationale behind the practice direction, and of course the Chamber always can overrule certain orders if and as long as the underlying rationale is met. And here I think it's the case, because the Prosecution starts for a better understanding, for reasons identified by the Prosecution, and it's for the Appeal Chamber, of course, to find out whether this is really a case for a summary dismissal or not, but to start with is a way which does not confuse or disturb the understanding of the brief, as such. And then they continue with a response to grounds 5 and 8, dealing with Mr. Martic's alleged participation in the joint criminal enterprise and the order he allegedly gave to attack civilians in Zagreb. And only then they continue dealing with grounds 1 to 4, which they regard as dealing in part again with grounds 5 to 8, however, more or less under the heading "Fair Trial." And thus I do not see how this brief can disturb the understanding of the brief, as such, and I personally cannot see how it makes the reply more difficult for the Defence on this. And we have indeed to balance, also taking into account the hierarchy of norms, that first of all it's a fundamental right to have the hearing in an expeditious way as possible, and not only expeditious for Mr. Martic, because he, in his opening remarks, highlighted how important it is for him, that he gets a decision on the Trial Chamber judgement, but also for the expeditiousness of those cases to come, as appeal cases to come. I think this fundamental principle of expeditiousness supersedes in this case the practice direction, because in this case, as a matter of fact, it's easy to understand and easy to have access to the reason why the Prosecution argued in this way. However, I would invite for the Prosecution in the future to respect the practice direction or request leave for deviating or departing from the order as set out in the Defence brief. In this case, in this concrete case, I think we all can accept the apologies of the Prosecution, and for the reasons I have given right now, the motion is rejected. Let me now turn to the dates when the reply brief will be due. I note that the Prosecution brief was filed on 25 February 2008. However, it was distributed only on 26 February 2008, and if there are no objections, and I can see none from the side of the Prosecution, the deadline runs as of 26 February 2008. So pursuant to Rule 113, the reply brief is due 15 days after the distribution of the response, which will bring us to 12 March 2008. So may I ask the Defence to respect this deadline, 12 March 2008. May I, in addition, ask the following: Both opposed to the Prosecution brief, the Defence brief was filed confidential, and thus it was justified that the Prosecution also filed the Prosecution brief in response confidential. But I recall that transparency of the hearings here in this Tribunal are of utmost importance, so that, in any event, we can deal, when we come to the appeals hearing, or we can deal in a public hearing with these two briefs. Thus, I not only invite but order both parties to please file a public version of both the Defence brief and the Prosecutor's response within one month as of now. This will bring us to -- let me check the calender. 29 March would be a Saturday, so no later than 31 March 2008. This is related only to the public version. You want to have the floor. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would just like to mention one thing in respect of the public redacted versions of the brief, and that is, if possible, the Prosecution would request that the appellant file the public version of his brief first, as he has designated the brief confidential. That will assist us in making sure that we make our redactions in a manner that's consistent with his brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the parties to deal with this matter together, without any further ordering by the Chamber. It's a party-driven system, I understand, so --

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have had a brief discussion about this before the commencement of the status conference today, and I'm certainly happy to speak to my colleague again afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Are you in agreement that we can continue on this basis, that both briefs are publicly available no later than 31st of March? Thank you for this. Then let's turn to further details on the time frame to be expected. The Appeals Chamber cannot give today an exact date on which the appeals hearing will take place, but please, and this is directed to both parties, please be prepared that the appeals hearing in all likelihood will take place before the summer court recess, which brings me to the question of the next status conference, as I know that it's important, in particular for Defence counsel, to know when he should appear here before the Tribunal. I would suggest, calculating 120 days as of now, that 27 June 2008 would be an appropriate day for the next status conference, bearing in mind that it might be that around these dates already, the appeals hearing, as such, may start. But to be on the safe side, I would kindly ask, would you be prepared to have the next status conference on 27 June 2008? Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. I just wanted to raise one brief issue, with your leave, and I hope that I have not interrupted your train of thoughts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can we just -- 27 of June is hereby scheduled. You will get the formal schedule order, in particular on the agenda and where it is to be held, in which courtroom. So we can agree that this will be on 27 June 2008. But this brings us already to the point you want to raise, namely, the miscellaneous other issues to be raised by the parties. You have the floor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence wanted to raise a brief issue and point to a problem. Mr. Martic has not received the Prosecutor's appeal in a language that he can understand. These proceedings are conducted in keeping with the Statute and the Rules, which prescribe that the accused should be provided with all the documents or the basic documents, at least, in a language that he can understand. Such documents are certainly the indictment, the judgement, and we fully believe that it should be the appeal as well. The judgement was drastic. The Prosecution's appeal is very elaborate. They are asking for even a harsher sentence. And this is something that the accused is vitally interested in, to read, and he is not able to do that because he has not received the document in a language that he can understand. So we would kindly ask Your Honour to take this into consideration and act accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before I give the floor to the Prosecution, I can see that Mr. Martic, himself, wants to address the Chamber. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to reply to your statement that this is not the place where states are prosecuted. I understand that. That's why I used the example of Dimitrov, because in the first instance the Trial Chamber has not taken into account any of our strong arguments, so I believe that you have not understood me properly when I said what I did. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As I said beforehand, we will -- and we have to take into account all the arguments put forward by you and your counsel in the briefs, and we will do, so you can be satisfied in a fair way. As regards first the matter of translation, may I hear the Prosecution on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution's understanding of the current practice is there is no entitlement to have the appeal brief translated into the language of the accused. Certainly, that entitlement exists for other parts of the record, and in particular the trial judgement which of course has been translated in this case. But if Your Honour would like further assistance on this, perhaps we can do that by way of a written submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm aware of the practice in the past, and what is remaining is, indeed, solely the reply to the Prosecution's response brief. And as I can see that Defence counsel in this case is able to discuss these issues with the client, I can see no merit in granting additional time, because having read carefully both briefs, I think that the main arguments are exchanged and that Mr. Martic knows, indeed, what is at stake. Thus, the interest of justice and the interest of expeditious proceedings also here prevail, and I think it is possible for the Defence, the Defence in the sense of the Rules, composed of Defence counsel and Mr. Martic himself, that they prepare the reply brief no later than 12th of March, 2008, as it is the practice in this Tribunal in relation, in particular, to reply briefs. Therefore, to be abundantly clear, your oral request for a departure of the time limit provided for in or set out in Rule 113 is hereby rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can understand your words, it seems that the Trial Chamber has not understood the Defence's words. I did not ask for any extension for the translation of the Prosecutor's reply. We don't need it. It has not been envisaged by the Rules. I was only talking about the translation of the Prosecutor's appeal motion. Mr. Martic only received the judgements with a six-month delay, and now we haven't received the appeal motion, and we believe that Mr. Martic should have that as one of the key elements in these proceedings. That was my proposal, and it had nothing to do with the Prosecutor's response. I was talking about the appeal motion by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let me clarify the following: You have received -- of course, there's no problem with the appellant's brief. Let's be clear on this, because it was filed by the Defence itself. Now you are claiming that the Prosecution response brief was not yet translated. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We are talking at cross-purposes here, and I'm sorry for being so direct. I am talking about the Prosecution's appeal against the first judgement. It has been filed. It is a voluminous document, and Mr. Martic has not received a translation. This is what I'm talking about. I'm not talking about any deadlines or extensions. We are in the situation that we have to work without a translation, but Mr. Martic has to be able to read the Prosecutor's brief. I'm not his tutor, I'm not the one who should interpret things for him. This was what I was talking about. I'm not talking about any extension of any deadlines. I'm talking about a translation of the Prosecutor's appeal brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification, and I think it's absolutely necessary that the accused gets a translation in a language he understands before the appeals hearing, and no doubt that the Appeal Chamber will take care that he has this document before the appeal hearing, because the rationale of the appeal hearing is also to advance additional arguments, if any, Mr. Martic has emanating from this brief during the appeals hearing. So, therefore, we will take care that well in advance a translation will be provided for Mr. Martic. Any other issues to be raised?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Nothing from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This concludes today's status conference, and we will meet again, if not earlier for the purposes of the appeal hearing as such, for the next status conference scheduled for 27 June 2008. I thank all of you for having contributed to this status conference. ---Whereupon the Status Conference concluded at 10.14 a.m. 23 24 25
